questions.text: A road sign is triangular with a red border. What is it telling you?

options.text: You must stop at the sign
You must not go beyond the sign
There is a hazard ahead that you should prepare for
The road ahead is one-way only

questions.explanation: The triangle is reserved for warnings, so the shape alone tells you to expect something ahead before you are close enough to read the symbol. Orders and prohibitions use circles instead.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code, traffic signs: warning signs

questions.text: You come to a sign that is eight-sided with a red background. What must you do?

options.text: Stop completely at the line, even if the road looks clear
Slow down and continue if nothing is coming
Give way only to traffic coming from the right
Sound your horn before moving off

questions.explanation: The octagon is the only sign of that shape, so it stays recognisable when snow or dirt hides the wording. Its instruction is absolute, and a rolling approach does not satisfy it.

questions.text: Most circular signs with a red border are there to do what?

options.text: Warn you about the condition of the road surface
Tell you what you must not do
Give directions to the town centre
Mark the end of a restriction

questions.explanation: A red ring is the standard way of showing a prohibition, so the symbol inside is something being taken away from you rather than offered to you.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code, traffic signs: signs giving orders

questions.text: What does a blue circular sign usually mean?

options.text: The road ahead is closed to all traffic
You are leaving a restricted zone
Parking is available nearby
There is something you must do, such as turn left or use a particular lane

questions.explanation: Blue circles carry positive instructions, unlike red-ringed circles which forbid. Blue rectangles are different again and only ever give information.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code, traffic signs: signs giving orders

questions.text: A white circular sign with a single black diagonal stripe appears at the side of the road. What does it mean?

options.text: The road ahead has no speed limit at all
The national speed limit applies for the type of road and vehicle you are driving
You may overtake anywhere beyond this point
Every restriction ends here, including parking rules

questions.explanation: No figure is shown because the limit depends on the road and the vehicle: 60 mph on a single carriageway and 70 mph on a dual carriageway for a car. It never means there is no limit.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a blue rectangular road sign?

options.text: To warn of a hazard ahead
To give an order that must be obeyed
To give information, such as directions to a motorway
To mark a temporary roadworks restriction

questions.explanation: Rectangles are the information family: motorway signs, parking signs and place names all use this shape. Blue circles look similar but still carry an instruction, not just information.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code, traffic signs: information signs

questions.text: You want to overtake, but there are double white lines along the middle of the road with the line nearest you solid. What must you do?

options.text: Overtake only if the road is clear for a long distance
Not cross or straddle the line
Cross the line if you are turning into a side road
Cross the line only at night, when it is easier to see oncoming traffic

questions.explanation: It is the line closest to your own side that decides whether you may cross: solid means no, regardless of what the line on the other side looks like or how clear the road seems.

questions.text: You approach a yellow box junction and the road ahead is congested. What should you do?

options.text: Enter the box and wait there until the traffic ahead clears
Not enter the box unless your exit road is clear
Enter the box only if you signal your intentions first
Enter the box as long as you are travelling straight ahead

questions.explanation: The markings exist to stop junctions from locking solid when traffic backs up. The one exception is turning right, where you may wait in the box if only oncoming traffic is blocking you.

questions.text: What do yellow zigzag lines on the road approaching a pedestrian crossing mean for a driver?

options.text: You must not park or overtake the leading vehicle there
You may park there for up to five minutes
They mark a bus lane in operation at all times
They only apply during school hours

questions.explanation: Both restrictions protect the same thing: a clear, unobstructed view of the crossing for both the pedestrian stepping out and the driver approaching it.

questions.text: A temporary sign at roadworks is triangular, red-bordered, and shows a symbol of a person with a shovel. What does it warn you of?

options.text: A permanent pedestrian crossing ahead
Roadworks ahead
A school entrance ahead
A cycle lane ahead

questions.explanation: Like any other warning triangle it is telling you to slow down and be ready to adjust for something temporary — here, workers and machinery that were not on the road last time you drove it.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code, traffic signs: warning signs

questions.text: You are taking the first exit, to the left, at a roundabout. How should you approach it?

options.text: Signal left on approach and keep to the left-hand lane
Signal right on approach and move left at the last moment
Stay in the right-hand lane so you can see further round
Approach without signalling and decide at the give-way line

questions.explanation: Getting into the correct lane early lets drivers behind read your route before you reach the give-way line, which is exactly where late lane changes cause collisions.

questions.text: You intend to take an exit past the twelve o’clock position at a roundabout. What is the normal procedure?

options.text: Signal left throughout and stay in the left-hand lane
Give no signal at all until you are on the roundabout
Signal right on approach, keep right, then signal left after passing the exit before the one you want
Signal right and hold that signal until you have left the roundabout

questions.explanation: Holding the right signal tells traffic waiting to join that you are still travelling round, and the late left signal is what releases them to move.

questions.text: What do broken white lines across the mouth of a side road mean?

options.text: You may drive straight out without slowing down
Traffic on the main road must give way to you
You must stop and apply the parking brake
You must give way to traffic on the major road before joining it

questions.explanation: Broken lines mean give way rather than stop, so you may keep moving if the road is genuinely clear. The duty to yield still rests entirely with you.

questions.text: You reach a junction with a solid white line across your lane and an eight-sided sign. What must you do?

options.text: Give way only if a vehicle is approaching
Stop behind the line every time, then move off when it is safe
Flash your headlights and continue
Sound the horn and edge out slowly

questions.explanation: That combination creates a legal obligation to halt, so it applies even when you can already see the road is empty. A give-way line would have been broken instead of solid.

questions.text: You are waiting at crossroads to turn right and an oncoming vehicle is also turning right. Which arrangement usually gives both drivers the better view?

options.text: Both drivers turn in front of each other, nearside to nearside
You always give way and let the other driver go first
You move into the middle of the junction and wait there
Turning behind each other, offside to offside, so neither car blocks the other’s view

questions.explanation: Passing behind one another keeps the road you are turning into visible to both drivers. Turning in front of each other hides oncoming traffic and pedestrians behind the other car.

questions.text: You are approaching a mini-roundabout. How should you treat it?

options.text: As a normal give-way junction, with priority to traffic already on the roundabout
As a stop sign, requiring a complete stop regardless of other traffic
As advisory only, since the markings are painted rather than raised
As a pedestrian crossing point with no vehicle priority rules

questions.explanation: The give-way-to-the-right rule is identical to a full-size roundabout; only the physical size and the flat, drivable centre marking are different, mainly to suit tight urban junctions.

questions.text: You reach a staggered junction where the road opposite is offset to the right. Which turn normally has priority over the other?

options.text: Traffic turning right into the offset road has priority over traffic turning right out of it
Whichever vehicle arrives first has priority regardless of direction
Traffic already emerging from the offset road always has priority
Neither turn has any priority — both must stop and negotiate

questions.explanation: Treat a staggered junction as two separate T-junctions rather than one crossroads: a vehicle turning right into the far road is effectively joining a new road, while one turning right out of it must give way first.

questions.text: The main signal at traffic lights is red, but a green filter arrow pointing left is also lit. What may you do?

options.text: Nothing — you must wait for the main signal to turn green
Proceed in the direction of the arrow if the way is clear
Proceed in any direction, since a green light is showing
Sound your horn to warn pedestrians, then proceed straight ahead

questions.explanation: A filter arrow only ever releases traffic for that one direction; the red main signal still applies to everyone going straight on or the other way.

questions.text: Parked vehicles are blocking your view as you emerge from a side road. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Edge forward slowly until you can see clearly, ready to stop
Sound your horn once and pull out at normal speed
Reverse back and take a different route
Wait for a pedestrian to check the road for you

questions.explanation: Creeping forward keeps your speed low enough to stop the moment a gap in the parked cars reveals approaching traffic, which a horn or a fixed speed cannot substitute for.

questions.text: You need to cross a dual carriageway from a side road, and the central reservation is too narrow for your car. What should you do?

options.text: Treat the crossing as a single manoeuvre and cross as soon as either carriageway is clear
Treat each carriageway as a separate road and wait in the side road until both directions are clear enough to cross in one go
Park in the central reservation gap and wait there regardless of width
Reverse into the side road and give up on the crossing

questions.explanation: If your vehicle would overhang into a live lane while waiting in the gap, stopping there is more dangerous than staying put — so treat it as one continuous crossing timed to the slower of the two flows.

questions.text: What is the national speed limit for a car on a motorway?

options.text: 60 mph
70 mph
80 mph
There is no fixed limit

questions.explanation: That figure is the maximum for cars and applies only where no lower limit is signed. It is a ceiling, not a target, and conditions often make it unsafe.

questions.text: When may you drive on the hard shoulder of a motorway?

options.text: To overtake slow-moving traffic
To take a phone call or check your directions
To rest during a long journey
Only in an emergency, or when signs show it is open as a running lane

questions.explanation: The hard shoulder is a refuge for breakdowns and a route for emergency vehicles, so any other use blocks the people who genuinely have no alternative.

questions.text: Which of these is not allowed on a motorway?

options.text: Pedestrians and cyclists
Vehicles towing trailers
Large goods vehicles
Motorcycles over 50 cc

questions.explanation: Motorways exclude anything that cannot keep pace with the traffic or that has no protection around it, which is why people on foot and on bicycles are barred.

questions.text: A red X is displayed on the overhead sign above your lane. What does it mean?

options.text: A speed camera is operating in that lane
The lane is reserved for buses and coaches
The lane is closed and you must move out of it
There has been an incident three miles ahead

questions.explanation: A lane is usually closed because people or a stopped vehicle are in it, so the sign is protecting somebody you cannot yet see. Driving past a red X is an offence detected by camera.

questions.text: How large a gap should you normally leave from the vehicle in front on a dry motorway?

options.text: One car length for every 10 mph
Enough to read its number plate
Half a second
At least a two-second gap, timed against a fixed point at the roadside

questions.explanation: A time gap grows automatically with speed, whereas counting car lengths badly underestimates the distance needed at motorway speeds. Double it as soon as the road is wet.

questions.text: You are joining a motorway from a slip road. What should you do?

options.text: Stop at the end of the slip road and wait for a gap
Build up your speed on the acceleration lane to match the traffic already on the motorway
Join at a steady 40 mph regardless of the traffic speed
Cross straight to the middle lane to get up to speed faster

questions.explanation: Matching speed before merging is what lets you slot into a gap rather than forcing traffic in the left-hand lane to brake or swerve for you.

questions.text: On a smart motorway with all lanes running as normal lanes, how do you know the current speed limit?

options.text: It is always 70 mph regardless of conditions
It is shown on overhead gantry signs and can change with conditions
It is printed on a fixed sign at the start of the motorway only
It matches whatever speed the vehicle in front is doing

questions.explanation: Gantry signs adjust the limit to smooth out traffic flow and respond to incidents ahead — a limit shown there overrides the usual national maximum until it is cleared.

questions.text: Your vehicle breaks down on a motorway with no hard shoulder available. What should you do?

options.text: Stop in the lane you are in and put on hazard warning lights
Try to reach an emergency refuge area, a slip road, or leave at the next exit if you can do so safely
Stop close to the central reservation and wait outside the car
Continue at reduced speed in the outside lane until help arrives

questions.explanation: A refuge area or an exit gets you and the vehicle out of a live traffic lane entirely, which a hazard-light stop in-lane cannot do on a road with no permanent hard shoulder.

questions.text: You want to leave the motorway at the next exit. When should you move into the left-hand lane?

options.text: As soon as you pass the exit before the one you want
In good time, generally from the 300-yard countdown markers
Only once you are level with the slip road
It does not matter, as long as you signal at the last moment

questions.explanation: The countdown markers exist precisely so drivers do not have to make a last-second lane change across live traffic — moving over gradually as they count down is the whole point of them.

questions.text: You are travelling in the middle lane of a three-lane motorway with no traffic to your left. What should you do?

options.text: Stay there, since the middle lane is for normal cruising
Move back to the left-hand lane once you have safely overtaken
Move to the right-hand lane to leave room for faster traffic behind
Stay there only if you are travelling at the speed limit

questions.explanation: "Lane hogging" in the middle lane forces faster traffic to undertake on the left, which is exactly the unsafe pattern that keeping left whenever possible is meant to prevent.

questions.text: Overall stopping distance is made up of which two parts?

options.text: Thinking distance and braking distance
Braking distance and the length of the vehicle
Reaction time and gear selection
Tyre grip and engine braking

questions.explanation: Ground is lost before the brakes are touched at all, which is why tiredness or a distraction lengthens the total even when the car, the road and the speed are unchanged.

questions.text: In good dry conditions, what is the typical overall stopping distance for a car travelling at 70 mph?

options.text: 53 metres
96 metres
36 metres
120 metres

questions.explanation: That is around 24 car lengths, and the figure climbs far faster than the speed does. About 21 metres of it disappears before you have even reacted.

questions.text: You begin to feel drowsy on a long motorway drive. What should you do?

options.text: Open a window and turn the radio up
Press on to your destination as quickly as you can
Leave at the next services or exit and rest before continuing
Move into the left-hand lane and slow to 50 mph

questions.explanation: Fresh air and noise mask tiredness for a few minutes without restoring alertness, so stopping is the only real remedy. Motorways offer almost nothing to keep the brain busy.

questions.text: What is the recommended minimum time gap to leave from the vehicle in front in good conditions?

options.text: One second
Two seconds
Four seconds
Ten seconds

questions.explanation: The two-second rule gives a rough, speed-scaled gap without doing maths on the move. In the wet, or when towing, at least double it to four seconds.

questions.text: How does wet weather affect your overall stopping distance compared with a dry road?

options.text: It has no real effect below 30 mph
It roughly doubles the braking distance
It only affects thinking distance, not braking distance
It reduces the distance, since tyres grip standing water

questions.explanation: A wet surface lets the tyres slide before they bite, so the braking portion of the stopping distance grows sharply — leave at least double the dry gap.

questions.text: You feel the steering go suddenly light on a wet road at speed. What is this a sign of?

options.text: Aquaplaning — the tyres are riding on a film of water
A flat tyre on the rear axle
Normal behaviour that needs no response
The power steering has failed completely

questions.explanation: Once a tyre loses contact with the road surface it cannot steer or brake effectively, so the correct response is to ease off the accelerator smoothly and let speed drop until grip returns.

questions.text: You are driving and a call comes in on your hands-free phone. What is the safest approach to hazard awareness?

options.text: Answer it, since hands-free calls are legally and mentally the same as no call at all
Answer it, but keep the conversation brief
Let it go to voicemail — a call still divides your attention even hands-free
Answer it only on quiet roads

questions.explanation: Hands-free removes the legal offence of holding a phone, not the mental distraction — studies on reaction times show a phone conversation slows hazard response whether or not a hand is on the device.

questions.text: You are driving past a row of parked cars near a school at home-time. What should you anticipate?

options.text: Nothing extra — treat it like any other stretch of parked cars
A child could run out from between the parked vehicles
Only that the parked cars might pull out without warning
That the speed limit no longer applies near schools

questions.explanation: Parked cars hide a small child completely until they step past the bumper, so the correct response is to slow down and cover the brake well before you draw level, not after.

questions.text: On a long motorway journey, how often is it recommended that you take a break to stay alert?

options.text: Every 30 minutes
At least every two hours
Only when you feel tired
Breaks are not necessary if the cruise control is set

questions.explanation: Waiting until you already feel drowsy means alertness has already dropped — a planned stop every couple of hours catches the decline before it becomes dangerous.

questions.text: Fog has reduced visibility to less than 100 metres. What should you do?

options.text: Switch on front or rear fog lights as appropriate, and slow down
Use full-beam headlights to see further
Keep your normal speed but leave a bigger gap
Follow the tail lights of the vehicle in front closely for guidance

questions.explanation: Full beam reflects back off the fog and worsens your own view, while fog lights cut through it for others. Speed still has to come down, since your effective stopping sight distance has shrunk.

questions.text: What is the minimum legal tread depth for a car tyre across the central three-quarters of its width?

options.text: 1.0 mm
2.0 mm
1.6 mm
3.0 mm

questions.explanation: Below that depth the grooves can no longer clear enough water from under the tyre, so wet grip collapses long before the tyre looks worn out.

questions.text: When does a car first need an MOT test?

options.text: On the third anniversary of its registration
After one year
After five years
Only when it is sold

questions.explanation: New cars are exempt at first because wear items are unlikely to have failed that early, and the test then becomes an annual requirement.

questions.text: What is the legal alcohol limit for drivers in England and Wales when measured in breath?

options.text: 22 micrograms per 100 ml of breath
50 micrograms per 100 ml of breath
80 micrograms per 100 ml of breath
35 micrograms per 100 ml of breath

questions.explanation: Scotland sets a lower figure, so the same drink can be lawful on one side of the border and not the other. Judgement is already impaired well below any limit.

questions.text: You are carrying a child under three years old in the front seat of your car. What must you use?

options.text: A normal adult seatbelt only
An appropriate child restraint
No restraint is required for short journeys
A booster cushion only

questions.explanation: Adult belts are shaped for adult proportions, so if the car is too small to fit a correctly sized child seat, that child legally cannot travel in the front at all — the seat is not optional.

questions.text: You must be able to read a vehicle number plate from what distance to meet the standard eyesight requirement?

options.text: 10.5 metres
20 metres (new-style plates)
30 metres
50 metres

questions.explanation: This is a legal minimum, not just good advice: failing it on the day of your test — or at any roadside check — means you are not fit to drive, glasses or not.

questions.text: Before a long journey, why should you check your tyre pressures when the tyres are cold?

options.text: Cold tyres give a falsely low reading that must be adjusted for
Driving warms the tyres and air, which raises the pressure reading
It makes no difference when tyres are checked
Warm tyres are more accurate than cold ones

questions.explanation: Checking after a drive would show a higher number than the tyre actually holds at rest, so you would under-inflate it once it cools back down — always check before setting off.

questions.text: Your windscreen washer bottle runs dry during a journey on a salted, muddy road. What is the main risk?

options.text: None — wipers work fine without washer fluid
The wipers may smear the screen and reduce your view instead of clearing it
It will damage the wiper motor within seconds
It only matters in freezing conditions

questions.explanation: Dry wiper blades drag grit and grime across the glass rather than lifting it off, turning a quick wipe into a smeared, harder-to-see-through windscreen at the worst possible moment.

questions.text: You have been prescribed a medicine with a label warning it may cause drowsiness. What should you do before driving?

options.text: Drive as normal — prescribed medicine is always safe to drive on
Take it only after you finish driving for the day
Follow the advice on the label and consult a doctor or pharmacist if unsure whether it is safe to drive
Halve the dose so it wears off faster

questions.explanation: Being prescribed a drug does not make it safe to drive on — the legal test is your actual impairment, and a pharmacist can tell you what that specific medicine does to reaction times.

questions.text: All passengers, including those in the rear, are required by law to do what while the car is moving?

options.text: Wear a seatbelt if one is fitted, unless legally exempt
Wear a seatbelt only on journeys over 20 minutes
Wear a seatbelt only if travelling on a motorway
Wear a seatbelt only in the front seats

questions.explanation: The driver is responsible for making sure any passenger under 14 is belted in; over that age, the legal duty to buckle up shifts to the passenger themselves.

questions.text: Your exhaust is producing thick blue or black smoke. What does this usually indicate?

options.text: Normal operation in cold weather
A mechanical fault that needs attention and could fail an MOT emissions check
The fuel tank is nearly empty
The tyres need replacing

questions.explanation: Persistent smoke usually points to burning oil or an over-rich fuel mixture — beyond the emissions failure, it is a sign the engine needs looking at before the fault gets worse.

questions.text: You are driving on a road with street lights but no speed limit signs. What limit applies?

options.text: 20 mph
30 mph
40 mph
60 mph

questions.explanation: Regular street lighting is itself the signal of a built-up area, so nothing needs to be posted. Repeater signs appear only where a different limit is in force.

questions.text: What is the national speed limit for a car on a single carriageway road?

options.text: 60 mph
50 mph
70 mph
40 mph

questions.explanation: A single carriageway carries oncoming traffic in the same strip of road, which is why the figure sits below the dual carriageway limit. Bends and junctions often make even that unsafe.

questions.text: What is the national speed limit for a car on a dual carriageway?

options.text: 50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
80 mph

questions.explanation: A central reservation separates the opposing flows, so the limit matches the motorway figure. Cars towing a trailer are held to a lower one on the same road.

questions.text: You see double yellow lines along the edge of the road. What do they mean?

options.text: Parking is free at any time
Waiting restrictions apply — check any nearby plate for the exact times
The road is a bus lane at all times
Parking is allowed only on Sundays

questions.explanation: The lines themselves only signal that a restriction exists; the actual times it applies are shown on a plate on a nearby post, and they vary a great deal between locations.

questions.text: You enter a one-way street. How can you tell which lane to use if you plan to turn right further along?

options.text: Any lane may be used regardless of your intended direction
Road markings and signs indicate which lane to take for each direction
You must always use the left-hand lane
You must always use the right-hand lane

questions.explanation: One-way streets often carry more than one legal direction of travel out of a junction ahead, so lane arrows and signs — not a fixed rule of thumb — decide the correct lane.

questions.text: You are stationary in traffic with the engine running. Is it legal to use a hand-held mobile phone?

options.text: Yes, as long as the vehicle is not moving
No — the restriction applies whenever the engine is running, not just while moving
Yes, if the queue has been stopped for more than a minute
Yes, for calls only, but not for texting

questions.explanation: The law is tied to the engine being on, not the wheels turning — switching it off, or being safely parked, is what actually removes the restriction.

questions.text: You are approaching a zebra crossing where a pedestrian is waiting to cross. Where must you avoid overtaking?

options.text: Overtaking restrictions do not apply near crossings
You must not overtake the moving vehicle nearest the crossing, or one that has stopped to give way
Only overtaking on the crossing itself is restricted
The restriction only applies to motorcycles

questions.explanation: Overtaking there hides the crossing and the waiting pedestrian from your view until the last moment, which is exactly the situation the rule is written to prevent.

questions.text: A bus at a bus stop ahead signals to pull out into traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Accelerate past before it moves off
Give way if it is safe to do so
Sound your horn to make it wait
Overtake it on the inside as it pulls out

questions.explanation: A bus re-entering traffic often has restricted visibility and a schedule to keep, so the Code asks other drivers to make room rather than forcing the bus driver to force their way in.

questions.text: You approach a level crossing and the amber light begins to flash, followed by red. What must you do?

options.text: Cross quickly before the barriers close
Stop and wait, even if the barriers have not yet come down
Sound your horn and proceed with caution
Reverse away from the crossing immediately

questions.explanation: The lights change before the barriers physically move, giving you a warning window — treating that window as extra crossing time is exactly how vehicles get trapped between the barriers.

questions.text: You hear a siren and see flashing blue lights approaching from behind. What should you do?

options.text: Stay in your lane and maintain your speed
Pull over where safe and legal to let it pass, without breaking traffic law to do so
Brake hard immediately, wherever you are
Speed up to clear the junction ahead of it

questions.explanation: You should make progress easier for the emergency vehicle, but never by mounting a pavement, crossing a solid line, or running a red light — the aim is to help, not to create a second incident.

questions.text: You are about to overtake a cyclist at around 30 mph. How much room should you allow?

options.text: Enough to pass without touching them
About half a metre
The width of a bicycle
At least 1.5 metres, and more at higher speeds

questions.explanation: Cyclists have to swerve around drains and potholes with no warning, and the air disturbance from a close pass is enough on its own to unbalance them.

questions.text: You are following a horse and rider on a country lane. How should you pass?

options.text: Sound the horn first so the rider knows you are there
Slow to no more than 10 mph and pass wide and slowly
Accelerate past quickly to cut the time spent alongside
Stay close behind until the rider waves you through

questions.explanation: A horse reacts to engine noise and sudden movement rather than to reasoning, so speed and closeness are the two things most likely to make it shy into the road.

questions.text: An elderly pedestrian is crossing slowly in front of you at the junction you are turning into. What should you do?

options.text: Wait patiently and let them finish crossing
Edge forward to encourage them to hurry
Sound your horn to warn them
Drive round behind them

questions.explanation: Pedestrians who have started to cross have priority, and an older person may not judge your closing speed or hear the car at all. Pressure is what causes them to stumble.

questions.text: You are turning at a junction and a motorcyclist is approaching. Why should you look especially carefully before turning?

options.text: Motorcycles are not allowed to have priority at junctions
A motorcycle's smaller size makes it easy to miss or misjudge its speed
Motorcyclists always give way to turning cars
It only matters if the motorcyclist has their headlight off

questions.explanation: A narrow silhouette is simply harder for the eye to pick out and its closing speed is easy to underestimate — a proper second look, not just a glance, is what catches it.

questions.text: A school crossing patrol steps out and displays a "Stop, children crossing" sign. What must you do?

options.text: Stop and wait until the sign is withdrawn and the crossing is clear
Slow down but keep moving if no children are visible yet
Stop only if a police officer is also present
Proceed if the patrol has not yet stepped fully into the road

questions.explanation: The sign carries the same legal weight as a red light — the patrol officer is managing children who may still be arriving at the kerb even if none are visible to you yet.

questions.text: You see a pedestrian carrying a white stick with a red band, or being guided by a dog wearing a distinctive harness. What does this indicate?

options.text: The pedestrian is a road safety officer
The pedestrian is deafblind
The pedestrian is a delivery worker
The pedestrian is training for an event

questions.explanation: A plain white stick signals visual impairment; the red band adds a hearing impairment on top, so extra time and a wider margin matter more than usual, since they cannot rely on hearing your car.

questions.text: You are behind a driver clearly displaying a green "P" plate. What does this tell you?

options.text: The driver has fewer legal rights at junctions
The driver has recently passed their test and may be less experienced
The driver must not exceed 50 mph anywhere
The plate has no meaning in current law

questions.explanation: It carries no special legal priority, but it is useful information: a newly qualified driver may react a little more cautiously or hesitantly, which is worth allowing for rather than pressuring.

questions.text: You approach a mobility scooter travelling on the road. How should you treat it?

options.text: As a slow-moving vehicle, giving it the same space and patience as a cyclist
As an obstruction to be passed as quickly as possible
It is illegal for mobility scooters to be on the road, so report it
As a pedestrian, so it has no right to use the road at all

questions.explanation: Class 3 mobility scooters are legally permitted on the road at a walking-to-cycling pace, and their low profile makes the same wide, patient passing distance you would give a cyclist just as important.

questions.text: You are driving along a country lane with no pavement and see pedestrians walking in the road ahead, facing away from you. What should you expect?

options.text: Pedestrians without a pavement are advised to walk facing oncoming traffic, so this is unusual and needs extra caution
This is completely normal and needs no extra caution
Pedestrians are never allowed to walk on a road without a pavement
They must be walking a large group, since solo walkers are banned there

questions.explanation: Walking facing traffic lets a pedestrian see and react to an approaching vehicle — walking with their back to it, as here, means they may not know you are there at all, so treat it as a higher-risk hazard.

questions.text: At traffic lights you see a marked cycle box (advanced stop line) ahead of the normal stop line. What should you do when the light is red?

options.text: Stop at the first white line and keep the box clear for cyclists
Pull into the box if there is space around the cyclists
Use the box only if turning left
The box is only a suggestion and can be ignored

questions.explanation: The reserved box lets cyclists position themselves ahead of queued traffic and get moving before it, well within a driver’s sightline — entering it defeats the entire purpose of the marking.

questions.text: When may you use your rear fog lights?

options.text: Whenever it is raining heavily
At any time after dark
Only when visibility falls below about 100 metres
Never on a public road

questions.explanation: Rear fog lights are far brighter than ordinary tail lights, so in clearer air they dazzle the driver behind and swamp your brake lights. Switch them off as the fog lifts.

questions.text: How does a wet road affect your stopping distance?

options.text: It has no measurable effect on a modern car
It shortens it because the tyres run cooler
It increases it by about a quarter
It can at least double it

questions.explanation: Water keeps the tyre from touching the surface directly, so the same pedal pressure does far less work. On ice the distance can stretch to ten times the dry figure.

questions.text: Why is coasting downhill with the clutch held down a bad idea?

options.text: It removes engine braking and reduces your control of the car
It uses noticeably more fuel
It carries an automatic penalty of six points
It makes the brake lights stay on

questions.explanation: With the drive disconnected the engine can no longer help hold the car back, so the brakes carry the whole load and steering response drops at the worst moment.

questions.text: The rear of your car begins to skid to the right. What is the correct initial response?

options.text: Steer to the right, in the direction the rear is sliding
Steer hard to the left to correct it immediately
Brake hard to stop the slide
Accelerate to regain grip

questions.explanation: Steering into the skid keeps the front wheels pointing the way the car is actually travelling; braking hard or oversteering the correction tends to snap the slide the other way instead.

questions.text: You are driving down a long, steep hill. Why should you select a lower gear rather than relying on the brakes alone?

options.text: It lets the engine help control your speed and reduces the risk of brake fade
It is required by law on every hill
It uses less fuel than braking
It has no real benefit over using the brakes only

questions.explanation: Continuous heavy braking on a long descent builds up heat until the brakes lose their bite — a lower gear shares that load with the engine so the brakes stay effective when you actually need them.

questions.text: Your car has ABS and you need to brake hard in an emergency. What is the correct technique?

options.text: Apply firm, continuous pressure to the brake pedal
Pump the brake pedal rapidly, as you would without ABS
Apply the handbrake at the same time as the footbrake
Brake gently to avoid triggering the system

questions.explanation: ABS is already doing the rapid release-and-reapply job for you many times a second — pumping the pedal yourself only fights the system and lengthens the car's stopping distance.

questions.text: You are overtaking a high-sided lorry on a motorway in strong side winds. What should you be ready for?

options.text: A sudden gust as you pass the gap at the front or rear of the lorry
No change, since the lorry blocks the wind completely
A drop in your own vehicle’s speed only
The lorry braking sharply for no reason

questions.explanation: The lorry shelters you from the wind while you are alongside it, then that shelter disappears abruptly the moment you clear the cab or the tail — hold the wheel firmly through that point.

questions.text: You are moving off in snow and the driving wheels are starting to spin. What should you do?

options.text: Ease off the accelerator and try moving away in a higher gear than usual
Press the accelerator harder to force grip
Select first gear and rev the engine hard
Switch off traction control and try again

questions.explanation: A higher gear delivers less torque to the wheels for the same throttle input, which is usually enough to stop them overpowering the thin layer of grip snow leaves you.

questions.text: When is the correct time to reduce your speed for a bend in the road?

options.text: Before you enter the bend, while the wheels are still pointing straight
While you are turning through the bend
Only after you can see the exit of the bend
It makes no difference when you brake

questions.explanation: Braking with the wheels straight uses all four tyres for slowing down; braking mid-turn asks the same tyres to slow the car and hold the cornering line at once, which is when grip runs out.

questions.text: Before reversing your car around a corner, what should you do first?

options.text: Check all around for pedestrians and other vehicles before you start moving
Sound the horn continuously while reversing
Reverse quickly to minimise the time spent in the manoeuvre
Rely only on the interior mirror throughout

questions.explanation: A reversing car has larger blind spots than a forward-moving one, and the check needs to happen before you commit to the manoeuvre, not partway through it once someone has already stepped into your path.

questions.text: What is the minimum level of insurance you must have to drive on a public road?

options.text: Comprehensive
Third party
Third party, fire and theft
None, if the vehicle is less than three years old

questions.explanation: The legal requirement exists to protect other people from injury or damage you cause, not to protect your own car, which is why the minimum leaves your own repairs unpaid.

questions.text: How long is a photocard driving licence normally valid before it must be renewed?

options.text: 3 years
5 years
10 years
For life

questions.explanation: The renewal is there to keep the photograph current for identification, so the driving entitlement itself carries on while the card is being replaced.

questions.text: Which of these must you tell the DVLA about?

options.text: A change of name or permanent address, and any medical condition that affects your driving
Every journey you make abroad
A change of car insurance company
Fitting new tyres to your car

questions.explanation: The licence record has to match reality so that correspondence and fitness-to-drive checks reach the right person. An out-of-date record can also invalidate your insurance.

questions.text: You sell your car. What must you do with the Vehicle Registration Certificate (V5C)?

options.text: Keep it yourself as proof you once owned the car
Fill in the new keeper details and send the relevant section to the DVLA
Destroy it, since it is no longer needed
Give it to your insurance company instead of the DVLA

questions.explanation: Notifying the DVLA at the point of sale is what moves legal responsibility for the vehicle to the new keeper — until that happens, problems with the car can still trace back to you.

questions.text: As a provisional licence holder, who is allowed to supervise you while driving a car?

options.text: Anyone with a full licence, of any age
Someone at least 21 who has held a full licence for that vehicle category for at least 3 years
Any front-seat passenger, licensed or not
No supervision is required if you display L plates

questions.explanation: Both conditions matter: the age floor and the three years of experience are there together so the supervisor is genuinely capable of coaching and intervening, not just legally qualified on paper.

questions.text: When must L plates (or D plates in Wales) be displayed on a car?

options.text: Only on motorways
Whenever a provisional licence holder is driving, clearly visible from front and rear
Only during a driving lesson with an instructor
Only in the first week after passing the theory test

questions.explanation: The plates warn other road users to allow for a less experienced driver — they have to be up every time a provisional licence holder is behind the wheel, not just in lessons.

questions.text: You are not going to use or keep your car on the public road for a while. What must you do if you do not have valid insurance and tax on it?

options.text: Nothing, as long as it stays on your own driveway
Declare a Statutory Off Road Notification (SORN)
Remove the number plates and store them separately
Notify your local council only

questions.explanation: A SORN tells the DVLA the car is off the public road so it can legally go without tax and insurance in the meantime — without it, both are still required even if the car never moves.

questions.text: You are planning to drive your own car in several EU countries. What is it sensible to check with your insurer beforehand?

options.text: That your policy provides at least the legally required cover abroad
Nothing — UK insurance never applies once you leave the country
That your MOT certificate is translated into the local language
That your driving licence photo is less than one year old

questions.explanation: UK policies vary in what they extend abroad — some drop straight to third-party-only cover outside the UK, so confirming the level of cover before you travel avoids a nasty surprise after an incident.

questions.text: A police officer asks to see your documents but you do not have them with you. What normally happens?

options.text: You are arrested on the spot
You may be given a set period, commonly seven days, to produce them at a police station
Your vehicle is permanently impounded
No further action is possible without the documents immediately

questions.explanation: Producing documents later at a station is the standard process precisely because most drivers do not carry every document in the car — it is a deadline to comply with, not an automatic penalty.

questions.text: Your car fails its MOT test with a "dangerous" defect. Can you still legally drive it away from the test centre?

options.text: Yes, as long as you drive slowly
No — driving with a dangerous defect is illegal even on an in-date MOT or none at all
Yes, if you only travel during daylight
Yes, but only on roads with a 30 mph limit or lower

questions.explanation: A "dangerous" result overrides everything else, including a previously valid certificate — the fault itself makes the car unfit to be on the road until it is repaired, whatever the paperwork says.

questions.text: You arrive at the scene of a collision before the emergency services. What should you do first?

options.text: Move all the casualties onto the verge
Take photographs for the insurers
Give the injured people a hot drink
Warn other traffic, for example by switching on hazard warning lights

questions.explanation: A second collision running into the scene is the most likely thing to happen next, and it would injure the people who stopped to help as well as the original casualties.

questions.text: An adult casualty is unconscious and not breathing. What should you do?

options.text: Give them water to drink
Open the airway by tilting the head back, then start chest compressions and call for help
Sit them upright against a wall
Wait for the ambulance without touching them

questions.explanation: The tongue commonly blocks the airway in an unconscious person, so clearing it may be all that is needed. Compressions keep blood reaching the brain until help arrives.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code annex 7: first aid on the road

questions.text: A motorcyclist has come off and is lying injured in the road. What should you do about the helmet?

options.text: Remove it straight away so they can breathe more easily
Remove it and use it to mark the scene
Leave it on unless removing it is essential, for example if they are not breathing
Remove it only once the ambulance has been called

questions.explanation: Taking a helmet off moves the head and neck, which can turn a spinal injury into a permanent one. That risk is only worth accepting when the airway itself is at stake.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code annex 7: first aid on the road

questions.text: Smoke starts coming from under the bonnet after a collision. What should you do?

options.text: Open the bonnet fully straight away to see the source
Get everyone well away from the vehicle before doing anything else
Pour water directly onto the engine
Keep the engine running to power the hazard lights

questions.explanation: Opening the bonnet feeds a fire fresh air and can flare it up in your face — getting people clear comes first, and firefighting is left to those with the training and equipment for it.

questions.text: You are involved in a minor collision but the other driver leaves without exchanging details. What should you do?

options.text: Report the incident to the police within 24 hours
Nothing, if there is no visible damage to your car
Wait a week to see if the other driver contacts you
Only report it if a passenger was injured

questions.explanation: The law gives a strict deadline for exactly this situation, so the incident is on record even without the other party’s details — leaving it unreported can leave you unable to claim later.

questions.text: A casualty at the scene is conscious but shows signs of shock — pale, cold, and sweating. What should you do?

options.text: Keep them warm and reassure them, without giving anything to eat or drink
Give them a warm drink to help them recover
Encourage them to stand up and walk around
Leave them alone so they can rest quietly

questions.explanation: Food or drink can be dangerous if they need surgery or lose consciousness shortly afterwards, and calm reassurance genuinely helps — being left alone or moved around does not.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code annex 7: first aid on the road

questions.text: You notice fuel has spilled across the road at the scene of an incident. What is the main hazard this creates?

options.text: It has no real effect on the road surface
It can make the road surface extremely slippery for other traffic
It only affects the vehicle it leaked from
It evaporates instantly and is never a hazard

questions.explanation: A thin film of fuel drops tyre grip dramatically, catching following traffic — and other pedestrians at the scene — off guard well beyond the vehicles actually involved in the incident.

questions.text: A casualty has a wound that is bleeding heavily. What is the first thing you should do, once you have called for help?

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the wound, ideally with a clean pad
Apply a tight tourniquet above the wound as standard practice
Wash the wound thoroughly with water first
Leave it uncovered so it can be assessed by paramedics

questions.explanation: Direct, firm pressure controls most bleeding on its own — more invasive steps like a tourniquet are reserved for bleeding that pressure alone cannot stop, not the default first move.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code annex 7: first aid on the road

questions.text: Your car breaks down on a busy ordinary road (not a motorway) and you cannot move it off the carriageway. What should you do?

options.text: Stay in the vehicle with your seatbelt on
Switch on hazard warning lights and get passengers out on the side away from traffic
Stand behind the vehicle to warn other drivers
Push the vehicle yourself without waiting for help

questions.explanation: Hazard lights make the stationary car visible early, and getting out on the kerb side keeps people away from moving traffic — standing behind the car puts you directly in the path of anything that fails to see it in time.

questions.text: At the scene of a collision, when is it appropriate to move an injured casualty?

options.text: Only if they are in immediate further danger, such as from fire or oncoming traffic
As soon as possible, to make them more comfortable
Always, so paramedics can access them more easily
Only once the police arrive and give permission

questions.explanation: Moving someone with an unknown injury risks making it worse, especially a spinal one — it is only worth that risk when leaving them where they are is clearly the greater danger.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code annex 7: first aid on the road

questions.text: Who is responsible for making sure a vehicle is not overloaded and that the load is secure?

options.text: The driver
The person who sold you the vehicle
The insurance company
Whoever helped you load it

questions.explanation: The duty follows whoever is in charge of the vehicle on the road, so it cannot be passed to the person who packed the car or hitched the trailer for you.

questions.text: How does a heavy load change the way a car drives?

options.text: It improves grip, so you can brake later
It has no effect as long as the load is inside the boot
It only matters at motorway speeds
Handling and steering change and the stopping distance gets longer

questions.explanation: The extra mass has to be slowed by the same brakes and turned by the same tyres, and weight carried high or well back also makes the car less stable in a swerve.

questions.text: You are towing a caravan and your normal mirrors do not show the road behind it. What should you do?

options.text: Rely on the nearside mirror alone
Fit suitable towing mirrors before you set off
Ask a passenger to watch behind for you
Drive closer to the centre line so you can see past it

questions.explanation: You need an adequate view of the road behind on both sides, and a caravan is usually wider than the car. Extended mirrors restore that view without changing your road position.

questions.text: You are loading a roof rack. How should heavy items generally be positioned?

options.text: Low down and towards the centre of the rack
As far forward as possible
At the rear, to keep the windscreen view clear
It does not matter as long as they are strapped down

questions.explanation: Weight sitting high and to one side raises the centre of gravity and unbalances the car exactly where you need stability most — in a hard corner or a gust of wind.

questions.text: You are towing a trailer on a single carriageway road. How does the speed limit compare with driving the car alone?

options.text: It is the same as for the car alone
It is lower than for the car alone
It is higher than for the car alone
There is no limit while towing

questions.explanation: A trailer adds weight and changes braking and handling, so the law caps your speed below the car-alone limit on the same road — the type of road does not change that reduction.

questions.text: You are carrying a full load of passengers and luggage. Why might you need to adjust your tyre pressures?

options.text: Heavier loads often require higher pressures — check the vehicle handbook
Tyre pressure never needs to change for load
You should always lower the pressure for a heavy load
Only the rear tyres need checking, never the front

questions.explanation: The pressures on the tyre wall assume a normal load — manufacturers publish a separate figure for fully laden driving, and running the wrong one hurts both handling and tyre wear.

questions.text: You have loose, heavy items in the boot of a hatchback with no parcel shelf. What is the main risk in a sudden stop?

options.text: They could fly forward and injure the occupants
They will only ever damage the boot lining
There is no risk if the boot lid is closed
The risk only exists in a fully loaded roof box, not the boot

questions.explanation: An unsecured object keeps moving at the car’s original speed even after the car itself has stopped — from the boot of a hatchback, that path leads straight into the back of the seats.

questions.text: Fitting a large roof box for a long journey is likely to have what effect on your car?

options.text: Increased fuel consumption and more sensitivity to crosswinds
Reduced fuel consumption from improved aerodynamics
No measurable effect on handling or economy
Improved high-speed stability

questions.explanation: A roof box adds drag and height, which costs fuel and gives side winds more surface area to push against — both worth planning for on a motorway-heavy trip.

questions.text: You have placed bags on the rear parcel shelf of your car. What should you check before setting off?

options.text: That they do not obstruct your view through the rear window
That they are visible to following drivers
That they match the colour of the interior
Nothing extra is needed if the boot is already full

questions.explanation: The parcel shelf sits right at eye level in the rear-view mirror — anything piled on it can blind you to exactly the traffic behind that you most need to see before changing lanes or braking.

questions.text: While towing, the caravan begins to snake from side to side. What should you do?

options.text: Ease off the accelerator gradually and reduce your speed
Brake hard and immediately
Accelerate to pull the caravan straight
Steer firmly in the opposite direction to each sway

questions.explanation: A gentle reduction in speed lets the trailer settle back in line; braking hard or fighting each sway with the steering tends to amplify the oscillation instead of calming it.

questions.text: The steering suddenly feels very light on a cold day. What is this most likely to mean?

options.text: A tyre has deflated
The power steering has failed
There is ice on the road surface
The road surface is about to change

questions.explanation: Ice takes away the resistance you normally feel through the wheel because the tyres have almost stopped gripping. Ease off and make every input as gentle as possible.

questions.text: You have to drive through a stretch of standing flood water. How should you do it?

options.text: Drive slowly in a low gear, keeping the engine speed up, then test the brakes afterwards
Drive through as fast as you can to create a bow wave
Stop halfway across and check how deep it is
Coast through with the clutch held down

questions.explanation: A steady engine speed keeps water out of the exhaust, and brakes come out of water wet, so gentle pressure is needed to dry them before you have to rely on them.

questions.text: You are crossing an exposed bridge in a strong side wind. What should you be ready for?

options.text: Your engine losing power in the gusts
Traffic behind you braking suddenly
The wind pushing you towards the verge only
Cyclists and high-sided vehicles being blown sideways into your path

questions.explanation: A gust moves light and tall vehicles far more than it moves a car, so the danger sits with what is around you rather than with your own steering. Leave extra room when passing them.

questions.text: You are driving at night on an unlit road with an oncoming vehicle approaching. What should you do with your headlights?

options.text: Keep full beam on so both drivers can see the road clearly
Dip your headlights in good time before you meet
Switch your headlights off completely
Flash your main beam repeatedly as you approach

questions.explanation: Full beam dazzles an oncoming driver and can leave them briefly unable to see the road at all — dipping in good time trades a little of your own view for both drivers staying safe.

questions.text: You are driving directly into low, bright sun and finding it hard to see. What should you do?

options.text: Use the sun visor, slow down, and increase your distance from the vehicle in front
Speed up to get past the glare sooner
Follow closer to the car in front so you can use its position as a guide
Switch on rear fog lights to warn traffic behind

questions.explanation: Low sun can hide a stopped vehicle or a pedestrian completely, so the sensible response is the same as for any other reduced-visibility hazard: slow down and leave more room to react.

questions.text: You see a sign warning of loose chippings on a newly surfaced road. What should you do?

options.text: Reduce your speed and increase the gap to the vehicle in front
Drive as normal, since chippings only affect motorcycles
Brake hard as soon as you see the sign
Straddle the white lines to avoid the loose surface

questions.explanation: Loose stones reduce grip for braking and steering, and a following vehicle can also throw them up at your windscreen — both risks are managed with lower speed and more following distance.

questions.text: It is autumn and the road is covered in fallen wet leaves. How should you treat this surface?

options.text: As having about the same grip as a dry road
As potentially as slippery as ice
As safer than a dry road, since leaves cushion the tyres
As a hazard only for cyclists, not cars

questions.explanation: A mat of wet leaves can behave almost like black ice, especially under braking or on a bend — the danger is easy to underestimate simply because leaves look harmless.

questions.text: You have just driven through a ford or deep puddle. What should you do afterwards?

options.text: Test your brakes gently as soon as it is safe to do so
Accelerate hard to dry the brakes quickly
Ignore it — brakes are unaffected by water
Pull the handbrake on firmly while still moving

questions.explanation: Wet brake discs and pads grip less well until the water is wiped or evaporated off them — checking with a gentle press confirms they have recovered before you need them for real.

questions.text: Heavy rain on the motorway is throwing up spray that reduces visibility for traffic around you. What should you do?

options.text: Switch on dipped headlights so other traffic can see you more easily
Switch on hazard warning lights while driving normally
Turn on rear fog lights, since visibility is reduced
Do nothing extra, since spray is a normal part of rain

questions.explanation: Dipped headlights in spray are about being seen, not about lighting your own way — fog lights are reserved for the much lower visibility of actual fog or thick falling snow.

questions.text: You spot a deep pothole in your lane just before you reach it. What is the safest response?

options.text: Brake and steer around it only if it is safe to do so, without swerving into another lane
Swerve immediately, regardless of traffic beside you
Accelerate over it quickly to reduce the impact
Stop in the lane and wait for a gap to go around it

questions.explanation: A sudden swerve can put you directly in the path of a vehicle you had not accounted for — checking it is genuinely safe first is what turns a pothole into a minor inconvenience rather than a collision.

questions.text: When should you signal?

options.text: In good time, whenever it would help other road users understand what you intend to do
Only when another vehicle is close behind you
Once you have already started the manoeuvre
At every junction, whether or not you are turning

questions.explanation: A signal is information for other people, not permission for you. Given too late, or when nobody is there to read it, it changes nothing about the safety of the manoeuvre.

questions.text: A driver coming the other way flashes their headlights at you. What does this mean according to the Highway Code?

options.text: They are giving you priority to go ahead
They are thanking you
They are letting you know that they are there
There is a hazard on your side of the road

questions.explanation: Flashing headlights carry the same single meaning as the horn. Reading them as an invitation commits you to a junction on somebody else’s guess about what is coming.

questions.text: You brake hard and feel the pedal pulsing under your foot as the anti-lock braking system works. What should you do?

options.text: Pump the pedal in time with the pulsing
Keep firm continuous pressure on the pedal until the car has slowed enough
Release the pedal and try again
Press the clutch and steer around the hazard

questions.explanation: The pulsing is the system releasing and reapplying the brakes far faster than any driver could. Easing off simply interrupts that cycle and lengthens the stop.

questions.text: A traffic light shows steady amber. What must you do?

options.text: Stop, unless you have already crossed the stop line or are so close that stopping might cause a collision
Accelerate to clear the junction before red appears
Treat it the same as a green light
Ignore it if no other traffic is visible

questions.explanation: Amber is a genuine stop instruction, not a warning to speed up — the only exception is when stopping safely is no longer possible, which is a narrow case, not a general licence to push on.

questions.text: A police officer is directing traffic at a junction with hand signals, while the traffic lights are also operating. Which do you follow?

options.text: The traffic lights, since they are automatic and unbiased
The police officer’s signals
Whichever one other drivers appear to be following
You may choose either, as both are equally valid

questions.explanation: An officer is usually directing traffic precisely because the automatic sequence is not coping with the situation — their signal always takes priority over the lights underneath it.

questions.text: Your brake lights have stopped working and you need to slow down on a busy road before you can get them fixed. What backup signal can you give?

options.text: An arm signal — arm extended downward and moved up and down
Sounding the horn continuously
Switching on the interior light
There is no recognised alternative signal

questions.explanation: The Highway Code still lists a small set of arm signals for exactly this kind of equipment failure, and drivers behind are taught to recognise them even if they rarely see one used.
questions.sourceRef: Highway Code, signals to other road users

questions.text: When is it acceptable to sound your horn while your vehicle is stationary in traffic?

options.text: Only to alert another road user to a danger
To tell the driver in front to move off more quickly
To greet someone you recognise on the pavement
Whenever you feel frustrated by the delay

questions.explanation: The horn is a safety signal, not a way to express impatience — using it to hurry another driver along is exactly the use the Highway Code specifically discourages.

questions.text: A red warning light shaped like an oil can lights up on your dashboard while driving. What should you do?

options.text: Stop as soon as it is safe and check the problem before continuing
Ignore it if the engine still sounds normal
Keep driving until the fuel tank is empty, then check
Turn the engine off while still moving

questions.explanation: A red dashboard warning (as opposed to an amber one) signals a fault serious enough that continuing to drive risks real engine damage — it is asking for an immediate stop, not a note for later.

questions.text: At a temporary roadworks site, a worker is manually controlling traffic with a "stop/go" sign. If it conflicts with a temporary traffic light nearby, which should you obey?

options.text: The worker’s sign, since a person can react to changing conditions the light cannot
The temporary traffic light, since it is the official signal
Whichever one shows first as you approach
Neither — proceed with caution based on your own judgement

questions.explanation: A person on site is normally there specifically because the automated signal is not handling that phase of the works safely — their manual instruction overrides it, just as a police officer’s does.

questions.text: After completing a turn, you notice your indicator has not self-cancelled and is still flashing. What should you do?

options.text: Cancel it manually as soon as you notice
Leave it, since it will cancel itself eventually
Turn the steering wheel sharply to reset it
Switch on the opposite indicator to cancel it

questions.explanation: A signal left flashing tells following drivers you are about to turn again when you are not, which can easily provoke them into pulling out — it needs cancelling the moment you spot it.

questions.text: A bus at a bus stop ahead of you signals to pull out into the traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Accelerate to get past before it moves
Sound your horn to claim priority
Move right and pass close alongside it
Give way if you can do so safely

questions.explanation: Buses stop constantly and struggle to rejoin a steady stream of traffic, so letting one out costs you a few seconds and keeps the whole service moving.

questions.text: A long lorry ahead of you is signalling left but has moved out towards the centre of the road. Why?

options.text: The driver has signalled by mistake
The driver is inviting you to overtake on the left
It needs the extra width to get round the corner, so you must stay back and not pass on its left
It is about to stop and unload

questions.explanation: The rear wheels of a long vehicle cut inside the path of the front ones, so the gap that opens on the left closes again as the turn is completed.

questions.text: You are on a roundabout and a long vehicle in the left-hand lane is signalling to continue round to the right. What should you do?

options.text: Overtake it on the right before it moves across
Hold back and give it room, as it may need both lanes to get round
Stay alongside it so that the driver can see you
Sound the horn to remind the driver of the correct lane

questions.explanation: A long vehicle often has to straddle lanes on a roundabout because of the way the trailer swings, and a car alongside sits exactly where the driver cannot see it.

questions.text: You are driving in a town with tram tracks running along the road. Why should you take extra care?

options.text: Trams cannot steer to avoid you and run to a fixed track
Trams always give way to cars at junctions
Trams are not permitted to share the road with traffic
Tram tracks have no effect on tyre grip

questions.explanation: A tram physically cannot swerve around a car blocking its path, and wet or shiny rails are also a genuine skid hazard for motorcyclists and cyclists crossing them at a shallow angle.

questions.text: You are behind a slow-moving tractor on a narrow country road with no safe place to overtake. What should you do?

options.text: Stay back and wait patiently for a safe, clear opportunity to overtake
Flash your headlights until the driver pulls over
Overtake on a bend as soon as you are frustrated
Follow closely so the tractor driver knows to speed up

questions.explanation: A tractor cannot simply speed up to suit following traffic, and pressuring the driver only increases the temptation to take a risky gap — patience costs you far less time than a collision would.

questions.text: An articulated lorry ahead of you is turning left into a narrow side road and has swung out to the right first. What should you do?

options.text: Hold back and allow it the room it needs to complete the turn
Overtake on the left through the gap it has created
Sound your horn to hurry the manoeuvre
Pull alongside on the right to save time

questions.explanation: A long trailer needs a wide swing to clear the kerb on a tight turn, and the gap it opens up on the left is exactly where the trailer will sweep back through a moment later.

questions.text: You are following a taxi that pulls up at the kerb ahead of you. What should you be ready for?

options.text: A passenger door opening suddenly, or the taxi moving off again without warning
The taxi always signalling clearly before every action
No particular risk beyond any other parked vehicle
The taxi being legally required to wait for you to pass first

questions.explanation: Taxis stop and start to pick up and drop off passengers far more often than ordinary traffic, and a rear door can open into the road with little or no warning — extra following distance buys you reaction time.

questions.text: You are behind a car clearly marked as a driving school vehicle with dual controls. It hesitates at a junction. What should you do?

options.text: Stay well back and be patient, allowing extra time for the learner to move off
Sound the horn to encourage them to go
Overtake at the junction to save time
Flash your headlights repeatedly

questions.explanation: A learner under instruction is expected to be more hesitant at junctions than an experienced driver — the marked car and dual controls are there so other road users know to allow for exactly that.

questions.text: A cyclist ahead of you is approaching a roundabout and stays in the left-hand lane while signalling to go straight across, past the first exit. What should you do?

options.text: Give the cyclist room and do not attempt to overtake alongside them on the roundabout
Overtake immediately, since cyclists must use the correct lane for their exit
Sound your horn to warn them they are in the wrong lane
Follow closely so other traffic can see the cyclist

questions.explanation: Cyclists are advised to keep to the left on a roundabout even when travelling past the first exit, precisely to stay out of the flow of lane-changing traffic — a driver overtaking alongside them removes that safety margin.

questions.text: You see a slow-moving vehicle ahead with an amber flashing beacon, indicating a wide or oversized load. What should you do?

options.text: Only overtake when you can see the road ahead is clearly safe to do so
Overtake immediately, since the beacon means it must give way to you
Assume the load is narrower than it looks
Flash your headlights so it pulls over first

questions.explanation: An amber beacon is a warning to other traffic, not an instruction to the load itself — it often cannot easily pull aside, so any overtake is entirely on you to judge as genuinely safe.

q-road-signs-01.text: Una señal de tráfico es triangular y tiene el borde rojo. ¿Qué te está indicando?

options.A: Debes detenerte en la señal
options.B: No debes pasar más allá de la señal
options.C: Hay un peligro más adelante para el que debes prepararte
options.D: La vía que viene es de sentido único

q-road-signs-01.explanation: El triángulo se reserva para las advertencias, así que la forma por sí sola te avisa de que hay algo más adelante antes de que puedas leer el símbolo. Las órdenes y las prohibiciones usan círculos.

q-road-signs-02.text: Llegas a una señal octogonal con el fondo rojo. ¿Qué debes hacer?

options.A: Detenerte por completo en la línea, aunque la vía parezca despejada
options.B: Reducir la velocidad y continuar si no viene nadie
options.C: Ceder el paso solo al tráfico que llega por la derecha
options.D: Tocar el claxon antes de arrancar

q-road-signs-02.explanation: El octógono es la única señal con esa forma, por lo que sigue siendo reconocible cuando la nieve o la suciedad tapan el texto. Su orden es absoluta y no basta con pasar rodando despacio.

q-road-signs-03.text: ¿Para qué sirven la mayoría de las señales circulares con borde rojo?

options.A: Advertirte sobre el estado del firme
options.B: Indicarte lo que no debes hacer
options.C: Dar indicaciones hacia el centro de la ciudad
options.D: Marcar el final de una restricción

q-road-signs-03.explanation: El anillo rojo es la forma habitual de expresar una prohibición, así que el símbolo del interior es algo que se te retira en lugar de algo que se te ofrece.

q-road-signs-04.text: ¿Qué suele significar una señal circular azul?

options.A: La vía que viene está cerrada a todo el tráfico
options.B: Estás saliendo de una zona restringida
options.C: Hay aparcamiento en las cercanías
options.D: Hay algo que debes hacer, como girar a la izquierda o usar un carril concreto

q-road-signs-04.explanation: Los círculos azules dan instrucciones positivas, al contrario que los círculos con anillo rojo, que prohíben. Los rectángulos azules son distintos y solo aportan información.

q-road-signs-05.text: Aparece al lado de la vía una señal circular blanca con una sola franja diagonal negra. ¿Qué significa?

options.A: La vía que viene no tiene ningún límite de velocidad
options.B: Se aplica el límite de velocidad nacional según el tipo de vía y de vehículo que conduces
options.C: A partir de este punto puedes adelantar en cualquier lugar
options.D: Aquí terminan todas las restricciones, incluidas las de estacionamiento

q-road-signs-05.explanation: No se indica ninguna cifra porque el límite depende de la vía y del vehículo: 60 mph en calzada única y 70 mph en calzada desdoblada para un turismo. Nunca significa que no haya límite.

q-junctions-01.text: Vas a tomar la primera salida, a la izquierda, en una rotonda. ¿Cómo debes aproximarte?

options.A: Señalizar a la izquierda al aproximarte y mantenerte en el carril izquierdo
options.B: Señalizar a la derecha al aproximarte y desplazarte a la izquierda en el último momento
options.C: Permanecer en el carril derecho para ver mejor el resto de la rotonda
options.D: Aproximarte sin señalizar y decidir en la línea de ceda el paso

q-junctions-01.explanation: Colocarte pronto en el carril correcto permite que quienes van detrás entiendan tu trayectoria antes de llegar a la línea de ceda el paso, que es justo donde los cambios de carril tardíos provocan colisiones.

q-junctions-02.text: Tienes previsto tomar una salida situada más allá de la posición de las doce en una rotonda. ¿Cuál es el procedimiento normal?

options.A: Señalizar a la izquierda todo el rato y quedarte en el carril izquierdo
options.B: No señalizar hasta que ya estés dentro de la rotonda
options.C: Señalizar a la derecha al aproximarte, mantenerte a la derecha y señalizar a la izquierda tras pasar la salida anterior a la tuya
options.D: Señalizar a la derecha y mantener ese intermitente hasta haber salido de la rotonda

q-junctions-02.explanation: Mantener el intermitente derecho indica al tráfico que espera para incorporarse que sigues girando, y el intermitente izquierdo tardío es lo que les permite entrar.

q-junctions-03.text: ¿Qué significan las líneas blancas discontinuas que cruzan la boca de una vía secundaria?

options.A: Puedes salir directamente sin reducir la velocidad
options.B: El tráfico de la vía principal debe cederte el paso
options.C: Debes detenerte y poner el freno de mano
options.D: Debes ceder el paso al tráfico de la vía principal antes de incorporarte

q-junctions-03.explanation: Las líneas discontinuas obligan a ceder el paso, no a detenerse, así que puedes seguir avanzando si la vía está realmente despejada. La responsabilidad de ceder sigue siendo enteramente tuya.

q-junctions-04.text: Llegas a un cruce con una línea blanca continua que atraviesa tu carril y una señal octogonal. ¿Qué debes hacer?

options.A: Ceder el paso solo si se acerca algún vehículo
options.B: Detenerte tras la línea siempre, y arrancar cuando sea seguro
options.C: Hacer ráfagas con las luces y continuar
options.D: Tocar el claxon y salir despacio

q-junctions-04.explanation: Esa combinación crea una obligación legal de detenerse, así que se aplica incluso cuando ya ves que la vía está vacía. Una línea de ceda el paso sería discontinua en lugar de continua.

q-junctions-05.text: Esperas en un cruce para girar a la derecha y un vehículo que viene de frente también gira a la derecha. ¿Qué solución suele dar mejor visibilidad a ambos conductores?

options.A: Ambos giran por delante uno del otro, pasando lado interior contra lado interior
options.B: Cedes siempre el paso y dejas pasar primero al otro conductor
options.C: Te colocas en el centro del cruce y esperas allí
options.D: Girar por detrás uno del otro, lado exterior contra lado exterior, para que ninguno tape la visión del otro

q-junctions-05.explanation: Pasar por detrás del otro mantiene visible para ambos la vía a la que se incorporan. Girar por delante oculta el tráfico que viene de frente y a los peatones detrás del otro coche.

q-motorways-01.text: ¿Cuál es el límite de velocidad nacional para un turismo en autopista?

options.A: 60 mph
options.B: 70 mph
options.C: 80 mph
options.D: No hay un límite fijo

q-motorways-01.explanation: Esa cifra es el máximo para los turismos y solo se aplica donde no haya señalizado un límite inferior. Es un techo, no un objetivo, y las condiciones a menudo lo hacen inseguro.

q-motorways-02.text: ¿Cuándo puedes circular por el arcén de una autopista?

options.A: Para adelantar al tráfico lento
options.B: Para atender una llamada o consultar la ruta
options.C: Para descansar durante un viaje largo
options.D: Solo en caso de emergencia, o cuando las señales indiquen que está abierto como carril de circulación

q-motorways-02.explanation: El arcén es un refugio para las averías y una vía de paso para los servicios de emergencia, de modo que cualquier otro uso bloquea a quien no tiene ninguna alternativa.

q-motorways-03.text: ¿Cuál de estos no está permitido en una autopista?
